Oracle's superclusters may soon not be so super. 
 
Decentralized and Distributed Training (The "Crowdsourced" Approach) 
 
Rather than gathering 100,000 GPUs in one physical building with its own power substation, new software frameworks are allowing companies to train AI across geographically scattered locations. 
 
• Distributed Orchestration: Advanced sharding tools like Microsoft’s DeepSpeed (ZeRO), Ray Train, and PyTorch Distributed allow models to be split into tiny fractions. 
 
• Overcoming Latency Constraints: Historically, training a single model across different data centers was impossible because internet speeds are too slow compared to Oracle’s physical RDMA cables. However, new algorithmic paradigms (like asynchronous gradient descent and consensus-based learning) allow GPUs to train a cohesive model even with slower network connections, opening the door for decentralized, grid-like AI training. 
 
 
Alternative Hardware paradigms (The "Post-GPU" Era) 
 
NVIDIA GPUs are general-purpose processors drafted into doing AI work. Competitors are building chips explicitly tailored to do only one thing, vastly outperforming GPUs on a watt-for-watt basis. 
 
• Neuromorphic & Analog Computing: Companies are developing analog and neuromorphic chips that mimic the human brain. Instead of constantly moving data between a processor and memory (which wastes 80% of a supercluster's energy), these chips process data directly inside the memory cells using variable electrical currents, cutting power consumption by up to 90%.
